verdict.summary: Registering a GitHub OAuth app is a single form under Developer settings. You get client credentials right away, and the docs describe no review or verification before other users can authorize it. The only review-style requirements are for an optional GitHub Marketplace listing. The real limits are rate limits and possible approval policies set by organization owners.
verdict.approval_wait: none (only an optional Marketplace listing has extra requirements; no timeline was found)

gates.name: Registered OAuth app (owner use)
gates.unlocks: You can authorize your own GitHub account through your app using its client ID and secret.
limits: Up to 100 OAuth apps per user or organization
With 'Expire user access tokens' on: access tokens last 8 hours, refresh tokens expire after 6 months without use

gates.name: Other users authorize the same app (no allowlist)
gates.unlocks: Any GitHub user you send through the authorize URL can grant access. The docs describe no test-user allowlist or limited mode.
limits: Users can edit the scopes they grant, so they may give less access than you requested
Org resources may need approval from an org owner (inferred, not verified)
Signing in the same user 10 times in one hour forces that user to re-authorize
gates.time_to_reach: Same as Gate 1, no extra steps

gates.name: Public use (optional GitHub Marketplace listing)
gates.unlocks: Anyone can authorize the app without review. A Marketplace listing only adds discoverability and billing.
limits: 2,000 access-token requests per hour per OAuth app
OAuth apps have lower API rate limits than GitHub Apps and do not scale with installs
Paid Marketplace listings need a verified-publisher org and at least 200 users for OAuth apps
gates.time_to_reach: Immediate for public use. No Marketplace review timeline was found.

steps.title: Sign in and choose the owning account
steps.detail: Sign in to GitHub. Decide whether your personal account or an organization will own the app. To register under an organization you need admin access to it.
gotchas: Each user or organization can own at most 100 OAuth apps.

steps.title: Confirm an OAuth app is the right choice
steps.detail: GitHub recommends GitHub Apps for new integrations. GitHub Apps have fine-grained permissions, per-repository access and higher rate limits. OAuth apps can only act on behalf of a user. Composio's managed GitHub OAuth already works, so register your own app only if you need your own branding on the consent screen, your own credentials, or narrower scopes.
gotchas: OAuth app rate limits do not scale with the number of users.

steps.title: Open the new OAuth app form
steps.detail: Click your profile picture (top right), then Settings > Developer settings > OAuth apps, then click 'New OAuth App'. If this is your first app, the button reads 'Register a new application'. For an org-owned app, start from the organization's settings instead.

steps.title: Fill in the registration form
steps.detail: Enter the Application name and Homepage URL (required), plus an optional description. Paste Composio's callback URL into 'Authorization callback URL'. You can add up to 10 callback URLs. Leave 'Enable Device Flow' off unless you need a headless flow.

values.label: Redirect URI
values.value: Composio callback URL (see the Composio callout on this page)

gotchas: The redirect_uri sent during the code exchange must match the configured callback URL.
The research found two different Composio callback URLs. Copy the exact one from your Composio auth config.

steps.title: Decide on expiring user tokens
steps.detail: 'Expire user access tokens' is on by default. With it on, access tokens last 8 hours and refresh tokens expire after 6 months without use. Each refresh returns a new refresh token. Leave it on if your token handling supports refresh; otherwise uncheck it.
gotchas: Turning this on later affects only new tokens. Existing users must sign in again to get expiring tokens.

steps.title: Register and copy the credentials
steps.detail: Click 'Register application'. Copy the Client ID and the client secret from the app's settings page and store them somewhere secure. There is no review step.

steps.title: Create a Composio auth config with your credentials and scopes
steps.detail: In Composio, create a GitHub auth config that uses your own Client ID and secret. Set the scopes as a space-delimited list. Composio's defaults are repo, user, gist, notifications, project, workflow and codespace. Remove any your agent does not need, because GitHub shows every requested scope on the consent screen.
gotchas: GitHub has no OIDC discovery document, so enter the endpoints manually.

steps.title: Run a test authorization with your own account
steps.detail: Start a connection and approve the GitHub consent page. The page shows your developer contact details and the data being requested. Then check that the granted scopes match what you requested.
gotchas: The authorization code expires after 10 minutes.
Users can reduce scopes on the consent screen, so handle partial grants.

steps.title: Share the connect flow with other users
steps.detail: There is no allowlist or approval step, so any GitHub user can authorize the app. If users need access to organization resources, an org owner may have to approve your OAuth app first. This is inferred and not confirmed by the docs.

steps.title: Plan for rate limits
steps.detail: Make sure your integration stays under 2,000 access-token requests per hour per OAuth app. Avoid signing the same user in 10 or more times in an hour, which forces re-authorization. If you expect heavy API use, consider a GitHub App.

steps.title: (Optional) Submit a GitHub Marketplace listing
steps.detail: You only need this if you want to be listed on GitHub Marketplace. A listing needs a privacy policy link, a support contact, a pricing plan, a logo, screenshots, webhooks for plan changes and cancellations, and a publicly available app. Paid listings also need a verified-publisher organization and at least 200 users. For org-owned apps, only an org owner can submit.

requirements.item: GitHub account (or admin access to an organization)
requirements.detail: The developer portal requires sign-in. Org-owned apps need admin access to the org.
Required fields on the registration form.
Up to 10 allowed. It must match the redirect_uri used in the code exchange.

requirements.item: Refresh-token handling if expiring tokens stay enabled
requirements.detail: Access tokens last 8 hours. Refresh tokens expire after 6 months without use.
Privacy policy, support contact, pricing plan, logo, screenshots, plan-change webhooks. Paid listings need a verified publisher and 200+ users.

scopes.effect: Full read and write access to public and private repositories, including org-owned ones. No review is needed, but users see this broad request on the consent screen.
Write-capable scope included in Composio's defaults. Drop it if the agent doesn't edit GitHub Actions workflows.
High-privilege scopes. No review gate was found, but request them only if needed, because users can refuse or reduce scopes.
Narrower read-only alternatives that make the consent screen less alarming.
Returns an expiring access token plus a refresh token even if the app isn't set to expiring tokens. Useful for testing a rollout of expiring tokens.

blockers.symptom: Code exchange fails after the user approves
blockers.cause: The redirect_uri doesn't match the app's configured callback URL, or the code was used more than 10 minutes after it was issued.
blockers.fix: Register the exact Composio callback URL and exchange the code right away.

blockers.symptom: Users get access errors on organization repositories
blockers.cause: Org policy may require an owner to approve third-party OAuth apps (inferred).
blockers.fix: Ask the org owner to approve the app, or use a GitHub App instead.

blockers.symptom: New tokens can't be generated, or users are asked to re-authorize
blockers.cause: The app exceeded 2,000 access-token requests per hour, or signed the same user in 10 times in an hour.
blockers.fix: Reuse stored tokens instead of re-running the OAuth flow. Consider a GitHub App for scale.

blockers.cause: 'Expire user access tokens' is on by default and the integration doesn't refresh tokens.
blockers.fix: Implement refresh handling, or uncheck the option in the app settings.

blockers.cause: The account already owns 100 OAuth apps.
blockers.fix: Delete unused apps or register under a different organization.

blockers.cause: The app doesn't meet listing requirements, for example no verified publisher, fewer than 200 users, or missing webhooks.
blockers.fix: Meet the listing requirements, or skip the Marketplace. A listing isn't needed for public use.

composio.note: Composio's managed GitHub OAuth works immediately with broad default scopes. Register your own OAuth app when you want your own name and contact details on the consent screen, your own client credentials and rate-limit pool, or narrower scopes. GitHub requires no review, so switching takes about 15 minutes. Copy the exact callback URL from your Composio auth config, because the research found two different Composio callback URLs. For heavy API use, consider a GitHub App instead.

evidence.claim: OAuth apps are created from Settings > Developer settings > OAuth apps via 'New OAuth App' (or 'Register a new application').
evidence.quote: In the upper-right corner of any page on GitHub, click your profile picture, then click Settings.

evidence.claim: An OAuth app can be registered under a personal account or an org where the registrant has admin access.
evidence.quote: You can create and register an OAuth app under your personal account or under any organization you have administrative access to.

evidence.claim: Form fields: name, homepage URL, optional description, up to 10 callback URLs, optional device flow toggle.
evidence.quote: You can enter up to 10 callback URLs.

evidence.claim: 'Expire user access tokens' is enabled by default.
evidence.quote: Expire user access tokens is enabled by default.

evidence.claim: Each user or organization can own up to 100 OAuth apps.
evidence.quote: A user or organization can own up to 100 OAuth apps.

evidence.claim: Scopes are requested via a space-delimited scope parameter and shown on the consent form.
evidence.quote: When setting up an OAuth app on GitHub, requested scopes are displayed to the user on the authorization form.

evidence.claim: Scopes include broad ones (repo, admin:org, workflow, delete_repo) and read-only variants (read:user, read:org, repo:status).
evidence.quote: Grants full access to public and private repositories

evidence.claim: offline_access requests an expiring access token and refresh token even if the app isn't configured for expiring tokens.
evidence.quote: Requests an expiring access token and a refresh token, even if your OAuth app is not configured to use expiring tokens.

evidence.claim: Users can edit scopes and grant less access than requested.
evidence.quote: users can edit their scopes, effectively granting your application less access than you originally requested.

evidence.claim: Authorization code flow uses github.com/login/oauth/authorize and /access_token; implicit grant not supported; device flow must be enabled.
evidence.quote: The implicit grant type is not supported.

evidence.claim: redirect_uri must match the configured callback; authorization code expires after 10 minutes.
evidence.quote: The temporary code will expire after 10 minutes.

evidence.claim: Expiring access tokens last 8 hours; refresh tokens expire after 6 months without use.
evidence.quote: The access token expires after eight hours, and the refresh token expires after six months without use.

evidence.claim: Enabling expiring tokens affects only new tokens; existing ones keep working.
evidence.quote: Enabling this feature does not cause existing tokens to expire

evidence.claim: OAuth apps are limited to 2,000 access-token requests per hour; 10 sign-ins of the same user in an hour triggers re-authorization.
evidence.quote: OAuth apps are subject to a rate limit of 2,000 access token requests per hour.

evidence.claim: OAuth apps have lower rate limits than GitHub Apps and do not scale.
evidence.quote: OAuth apps have lower rate limits and do not scale.

evidence.claim: GitHub recommends GitHub Apps; OAuth apps can only act on behalf of a user.
evidence.quote: OAuth apps can only act on behalf of a user while GitHub Apps can either act on behalf of a user or independently of a user.

evidence.claim: The consent page shows developer contact information and requested data.
evidence.quote: you'll see a page with the developer contact information and a list of the specific data that's being requested.

evidence.claim: Org owners may need to approve third-party OAuth apps before members can use them with org resources (not verified).
No review or verification step for OAuth app registration is described; the form returns client credentials immediately.
Marketplace listings need a privacy policy, support contact, pricing plan, logo, screenshots; paid listings need a verified publisher and 200+ users for OAuth apps.
evidence.quote: OAuth apps should have a minimum of 200 users.

evidence.claim: Marketplace apps need plan-change/cancellation webhooks and must be publicly available.
evidence.quote: Apps must have webhook events set up to notify the publisher of any plan changes or cancellations

evidence.claim: Only organization owners can submit Marketplace listings for org-owned apps.
evidence.quote: only organization owners can create and submit listings in GitHub Marketplace.

evidence.claim: github.com/settings/developers requires sign-in.
evidence.quote: Sign in to GitHub

evidence.claim: GitHub has no OIDC discovery document at /.well-known/openid-configuration (404).
Composio offers managed OAuth for GitHub with the GitHub authorize/token URLs and default scopes.

open_questions: Which Composio callback URL to register: the probe returned backend.composio.dev/api/v3/toolkits/auth/callback, but the toolkit lookup returned backend.composio.dev/api/v1/auth-apps/add. Copy the exact URL shown in your Composio auth config.
Whether org owners must approve third-party OAuth apps before members can use them with org resources was not confirmed.
Whether GitHub requires a verified email, 2FA or a paid plan to create OAuth apps was not confirmed.
No timeline was found for GitHub Marketplace listing review or publisher verification.
An unfetched 'Privileged apps' doc page might describe an extra review path for OAuth apps.
The exact redirect URI matching rules (subdomains, ports, paths) and the location of the device flow toggle in the settings of an existing app were not fully verified.
